title: Worison, Unkechaug Whaler
summary: Worison appears in seventeenth-century Unkechaug whaling and land records under several spellings, including Waishone, Warishone, and Areshunk.
content:
Worison, also written Waishone, Warishone, or Areshunk, was a seventeenth-century Unkechaug whaler and kinsman connected with Watchogue Neck and early shore-whaling contracts.12

Historical Context

English whaling contracts identify Worison as one of the first recorded Unkechaug whalers, signing agreements with John Cooper in the winter of 1676-1677.1

The records show Native labor and expertise in the early Long Island whale fishery while also placing that work inside English-controlled contracts and profit sharing.1

In 1680, a land description remembered him at a neck of land west of Watchogue, where Mahue described Warishone as his kinsman.2

References

  1. John A. Strong, The Unkechaug Indians of Eastern Long Island: A History, pp. 76, 96.
  2. William Wallace Tooker, Indian Place-Names on Long Island and Islands Adjacent, p. 20.
why_this_matters: Worison makes visible Unkechaug maritime labor and expertise in seventeenth-century Long Island. His record connects land, kinship, and whaling at a time when Native people worked within and against colonial economic systems.
